**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections: SECTION A (1800 - 1922), questions 1 to 4; SECTION B (1922 - 1961), questions 5 to 8; SECTION C (1961 to present), questions 9 to 12.

Points : chaque question imprime « (25 marks) » et le sujet dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` vaut donc 25 pour chaque question. Aucun écart constaté entre les points imprimés.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les 12 questions) : filigrane et publicités gcerevision.com sans conséquence sur la lisibilité ; aucune question n'est coupée ni illisible. Page de garde vérifiée : « JUNE 2020 », ADVANCED LEVEL, History, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, trois heures.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire historiographique, sans accès à un manuel pendant la rédaction ; aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée. Les dates et les faits cités sont ceux de l'historiographie courante du Cameroun, mais n'ont pas pu être recoupés avec une source écrite : à relire par un historien avant publication.

Faits cités de mémoire et à recouper : plans quinquennaux (1971-1976, 1976-1981, 1981-1986), « libéralisme planifié », « révolution verte », sociétés d'État (SODECOTON, SEMRY, SOCAPALM, HEVECAM), chemin de fer transcamerounais jusqu'à Ngaoundéré (1974), Camair (1971), centres universitaires de 1977, début de l'exploitation pétrolière en 1977, démission d'Ahidjo en novembre 1982, opacité budgétaire des revenus pétroliers. Aucun chiffre de croissance ou de dette n'est donné.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Assess the attempts by President Ahidjo at resolving the socio-economic problems of Cameroon between 1972 and 1982.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** After the federation was replaced by the unitary United Republic of Cameroon (referendum of 20 May 1972), President Ahmadou Ahidjo governed until his resignation in November 1982. The country he ruled was one of the poorer countries of Africa. Its socio-economic problems included dependence on a few export crops (cocoa, coffee, cotton, bananas, timber), low productivity of peasant agriculture, weak industry and infrastructure, regional inequalities between the North, the Centre-South, the West and the Anglophone provinces, rural poverty and drift to the towns, and shortages of schools, hospitals and trained staff. Ahidjo's government tried to deal with these problems through planning, agricultural policy, infrastructure, industrialisation and, from the late 1970s, the use of oil revenue. This essay assesses how far these attempts succeeded.

**1. The attempts**

- **National development planning.** Ahidjo relied on successive Five-Year Development Plans (the third covered about 1971-1976 and the fourth about 1976-1981, with the fifth beginning in 1981), directed by the state and following his doctrine of "planned liberalism", which combined state direction with private enterprise and foreign investment. The plans aimed at economic growth, self-sufficiency in food and balanced regional development.
- **The abolition of the federation (1972).** The unitary state was presented as a way of promoting national unity and a more efficient use of resources, avoiding duplication and creating a single national economic space.
- **Agricultural policy.** The government made agriculture the base of development and in the 1970s launched what was called the "Green Revolution", with state agencies to develop particular crops and regions: for example SODECOTON (cotton, in the North), SEMRY (rice, in the Far North, from 1971), SOCAPALM (palm oil) and HEVECAM (rubber), and farmers received help in credit, inputs and extension. Marketing boards and cooperatives bought and exported cocoa and coffee. The aim was to raise incomes and food production.
- **Infrastructure.** The government built roads, extended the Transcameroon railway from Yaounde to Ngaoundere (reached in 1974) to open the North and link it to the coast, developed ports and airports, set up the national airline (Cameroon Airlines, 1971) and built dams and hydroelectric stations (Edea and Song Loulou, and the Lagdo dam on the Benue) to meet the demand for energy.
- **Industrialisation.** The state encouraged import-substituting and processing industries (textiles, cement, food processing, brewing, aluminium at Edea) through public enterprises and partnerships with foreign firms, and the National Investment Corporation (SNI) and other state bodies took shares in them.
- **Oil.** The commercial exploitation of oil began in 1977, and oil revenue grew in the following years; the government used part of it to finance projects and public services, and it also built up reserves.
- **Social policy: education and health.** Schools, colleges and health centres were multiplied, the University of Yaounde was joined by new university centres (created in 1977 at Douala, Dschang, Buea and Ngaoundere), and the government tried to reduce regional inequalities by the policy of "regional balance" in school admissions and public service appointments.
- **National integration.** Single-party rule through the Cameroon National Union (CNU) was intended to unite the regions and keep social peace.

**2. Assessment of the success**

*Achievements.* Cameroon enjoyed political stability and fairly steady economic growth in this period, with expansion of agriculture, new industries and infrastructure. Compared with many African countries it avoided the worst crises, was largely self-sufficient in food and kept relatively low external debt. Oil provided funds towards the end of the period. Education and health services grew, and the railway and roads opened the interior.

*Limits and failures.*
- **Dependence on primary exports and on world prices.** The economy remained based on the export of raw materials and on foreign capital and expertise, and so was vulnerable to falling prices, a weakness that was exposed after Ahidjo's departure.
- **Regional and social inequalities.** Development remained concentrated in the towns and in some regions (Douala, Yaounde, the cocoa and coffee zones, the plantation areas), and the Anglophone regions and the far North continued to complain of neglect. Rural poverty and migration to the towns increased.
- **Weak state enterprises and management.** Many public enterprises were inefficient, and the large role of the state and of an administrative elite limited private initiative and the growth of an indigenous business class.
- **Lack of transparency.** Oil revenue was handled largely outside the normal budget, which made it difficult to judge how it was used, and critics accused the government of excessive secrecy (the later economic problems of the 1980s made this criticism more serious).
- **Authoritarian politics.** The single party and the restriction of political liberty limited criticism and participation in development.
- **Limited achievement in food, education and employment.** The supply of trained manpower, jobs for the young and the quality of public services remained insufficient for a rapidly growing population.

**Conclusion.** Between 1972 and 1982 Ahidjo made serious and partly successful attempts to solve Cameroon's socio-economic problems through planning, the development of agriculture, infrastructure and industry, and the use of oil revenue, achieving stability and growth. But the economy remained dependent on a few exports, regional and social inequalities persisted, and the state-centred, authoritarian management had weaknesses that appeared in the economic crisis after 1985. The attempts were therefore **a moderate success**: they improved material conditions in many areas but did not resolve the structural problems of underdevelopment.
